Set the derivative equal to zero, divide by $\cos(2x)$, and solve $\tan(2x) = -1$ for $x \in [0, \pi/2]$.
walkthrough:
Differentiate $y = \mathrm{e}^{2x}\sin(2x)$ with respect to $x$ using the product rule:
$$u = \mathrm{e}^{2x} \implies u' = 2\mathrm{e}^{2x}$$
$$v = \sin(2x) \implies v' = 2\cos(2x)$$
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 2\mathrm{e}^{2x}\sin(2x) + 2\mathrm{e}^{2x}\cos(2x) = 2\mathrm{e}^{2x}(\sin(2x) + \cos(2x))$$

Set $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 0$ to find stationary points:
$$2\mathrm{e}^{2x}(\sin(2x) + \cos(2x)) = 0$$
Since $\mathrm{e}^{2x} > 0$ for all real $x$, divide by $2\mathrm{e}^{2x}$:
$$\sin(2x) + \cos(2x) = 0$$

Calculate the exact $y$-coordinate by substituting $x = \dfrac{3\pi}{8}$ into the curve equation:
$$y = \mathrm{e}^{2(3\pi/8)}\sin\left(2 \times \dfrac{3\pi}{8}\right) = \mathrm{e}^{3\pi/4}\sin\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right)$$
Since $\sin\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$:
$$y = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\mathrm{e}^{3\pi/4}$$

State the exact coordinates of the stationary point:
$$\left( \dfrac{3\pi}{8}, \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\mathrm{e}^{3\pi/4} \right)$$

ai_rubric.Finding Stationary Points: Uses product rule correctly (M1). Obtains $2e^{2x}\sin 2x + 2e^{2x}\cos 2x$ (A1). Equates derivative to zero and solves for $x$ (M1). Obtains $x = 3\pi/8$ (A1). Obtains $y = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}e^{3\pi/4}$ (A1).
